questions.stem: Which definition matches diffusion?

options.text: Net movement of particles from higher to lower concentration
options.explanation: That is the gradient-driven movement the specification describes.

options.text: Movement of water across a partially permeable membrane
options.explanation: That is osmosis, water's special case.
Diffusion is passive; energy is not spent.

options.text: Movement of particles against a gradient
options.explanation: Diffusion never runs uphill.

questions.stem: How does an amoeba exchange gases?

options.explanation: Gas exchange is passive diffusion.

options.text: By diffusion straight across its cell membrane
options.explanation: A single cell needs no organ; its surface does everything.
Stomata belong to leaves, not amoeba.

options.text: Using lungs inherited from larger cells
options.explanation: Amoeba has no organs at all.

questions.stem: What is the gas exchange organ in humans?

options.explanation: Leaves are the plant's exchange surface.
The heart pumps blood; it exchanges nothing with the air.
Lungs are the human gas exchange organ named here.
Gills belong to fish.

questions.stem: Which feature of an exchange surface speeds diffusion?

options.explanation: Thickness slows exchange; exchange surfaces are thin.
Moisture helps gases dissolve and cross.
Small area reduces the exchange rate.
Thin barriers shorten each particle's journey.

questions.stem: Why do animals ventilate their exchange surfaces?

options.text: To keep the concentration gradients steep for faster exchange
options.explanation: Fresh air or water refreshes the gradient that diffusion feeds on.
Cooling is a separate role; ventilation's exchange job is gradient renewal.

options.text: To filter dust from the air
options.explanation: Filtering is a defensive extra, not the exchange reason.

options.text: Because diffusion would stop without movement
options.explanation: Diffusion slows but does not stop; the point is keeping it fast.

questions.stem: Define diffusion in one sentence.
questions.modelAnswer: Diffusion is the net drift of particles from where they are more concentrated to where they are less so, down a gradient.

questions.stem: Name the gas exchange organs of fish, humans and plants.
questions.modelAnswer: Fish use gills, humans use lungs, and plants use leaves and roots.

questions.stem: Explain why single-celled organisms need no exchange organs.
questions.modelAnswer: Because their whole surface touches the environment, so every part of the membrane can exchange directly and the distances involved are tiny; multicellular bodies bury their inner cells, which is why organs become necessary.

questions.stem: A spherical cell grows to ten times its diameter. Use surface-area reasoning to predict its gas exchange problem.
questions.modelAnswer: Volume grows with the cube of diameter but surface with only the square, so demand for gases far outstrips the membrane able to supply them; diffusion distance to the centre also lengthens, so the cell would suffocate inside unless it found an exchange organ or split.

questions.stem: Which gas does a respiring cell consume?

options.explanation: Water is a product of respiration, not a gas it consumes.
Aerobic respiration takes in oxygen and releases carbon dioxide.
Carbon dioxide is the product, not the reactant.
Nitrogen takes no part in respiration.

questions.stem: At night, which direction does carbon dioxide move in a leaf?

options.explanation: Respiration continues, so the exchange continues.
Gas exchange happens at the leaf's surfaces.

options.text: Out of the leaf, down its gradient
options.explanation: Respiring cells make the inside rich, so the gas leaves.
That would need photosynthesis, which has stopped.

questions.stem: Why does oxygen keep diffusing into a respiring leaf all night?

options.text: Because the leaf stores oxygen in vacuoles
options.explanation: Nothing stores oxygen; consumption explains the low level.

options.text: Because the stomata pump air in
options.explanation: Stomata are passive pores; nothing pumps.

options.text: Because oxygen becomes more concentrated inside
options.explanation: Inside stays LOW; that is the whole point.

options.text: The respiring cells keep internal oxygen low, so the gradient persists
options.explanation: Constant consumption holds the inside below the outside.

questions.stem: What would happen to gas exchange if a leaf's cells stopped respiring?

options.text: Both gradients would collapse and exchange would cease
options.explanation: No consumption, no low oxygen; no output, no high carbon dioxide.
Without consumption there is no gradient to pull it.

options.text: Only carbon dioxide would still leave
options.explanation: Its gradient depends on respiration too.

options.text: Exchange would continue by active transport
options.explanation: The exchange is passive and gradient-dependent.

questions.stem: During the day, which process usually dominates a green leaf's gas exchange?

options.explanation: Transpiration is water loss, not the gas pair's exchange.

options.text: Photosynthesis, so the leaf takes in carbon dioxide overall
options.explanation: In sufficient light photosynthesis outruns respiration and reverses the flows.
Respiration runs but is outrun; the net flow favours photosynthesis's pattern.
Both run; photosynthesis simply outpaces.

questions.stem: Name the two gases exchanged during respiration.
questions.modelAnswer: Oxygen, taken in, and carbon dioxide, released.

questions.stem: State the direction of each gas's movement at night.
questions.modelAnswer: Oxygen enters the leaf while carbon dioxide leaves it.

questions.stem: Explain why respiration is described as continuous while photosynthesis is not.
questions.modelAnswer: Because every living cell needs energy every moment, and respiration supplies it, whereas photosynthesis depends on light and halts in darkness; the gas exchange of respiration therefore runs around the clock while photosynthesis's runs only in daylight.

questions.stem: A sealed jar contains a plant in complete darkness overnight. Predict the air's carbon dioxide level by morning and explain.
questions.modelAnswer: The carbon dioxide level rises: with no light the plant only respires, releasing carbon dioxide into the sealed air while consuming its oxygen, and with nowhere for the gas to diffuse the concentration climbs steadily.

questions.stem: Which gas does photosynthesis consume?

options.explanation: Nitrogen plays no role here.
Glucose is the sugar made by photosynthesis, not a gas it consumes.
Carbon dioxide is photosynthesis's raw material.
Oxygen is the product; carbon dioxide is consumed.

questions.stem: During photosynthesis, which way does oxygen move?

options.explanation: That is respiration's direction at night.

options.text: It stays put inside the chloroplasts
options.explanation: Gas diffuses; some is used by respiration, the rest leaves.

options.text: Through the roots into the soil
options.explanation: Gas exchange happens at the leaf.

options.text: Out of the leaf, down its gradient
options.explanation: Produced inside, oxygen builds up and leaves.

questions.stem: Why does carbon dioxide keep flowing into a photosynthesising leaf?

options.text: The photosynthesising cells keep internal carbon dioxide low
options.explanation: Constant consumption maintains the inward gradient.

options.text: Because the leaf pumps air inwards
options.explanation: Nothing pumps; diffusion does the work.

options.text: Because carbon dioxide dissolves in the waxy cuticle
options.explanation: The cuticle is a barrier, not an entry route.

options.text: Because the leaf stores it for night
options.explanation: It is consumed immediately, not stored.

questions.stem: What happens to the oxygen made during photosynthesis?

options.text: It is converted back into carbon dioxide
options.explanation: That reversal is respiration, not a direct conversion here.

options.text: Some is used by respiration and the surplus diffuses out
options.explanation: Respiration runs underneath and spends some of the supply.

options.text: All of it is stored in the vacuole
options.explanation: Nothing stores oxygen; the surplus leaves.
Respiration claims a share first.

questions.stem: When photosynthesis and respiration run at similar rates, what is the net gas exchange?

options.explanation: That is the darkness outcome.
Both processes still run; only the net shrinks.

options.text: Roughly zero — photosynthesis and respiration run at similar rates
options.explanation: Parity between the processes flattens the net flows.
That needs photosynthesis well ahead, which dim light prevents.

questions.stem: State the direction of each gas's movement in bright light.
questions.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide enters the leaf while oxygen leaves it.

questions.stem: Name the organelle where photosynthesis happens.
Explain why a leaf in dim light may show almost no net gas exchange.
questions.modelAnswer: Because photosynthesis's consumption of carbon dioxide and release of oxygen nearly match respiration's opposite flows; the two processes cancel almost exactly, so neither gas shows a clear net movement.

questions.stem: A greenhouse adds morning light gradually from dark to bright. Describe how the leaf's gas exchange shifts across the morning.
questions.modelAnswer: In darkness only respiration runs: oxygen in, carbon dioxide out. As light strengthens photosynthesis wakes and trims those flows; near parity the net exchange almost vanishes; in full light photosynthesis dominates and the flows reverse — carbon dioxide in, oxygen out.
